newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian election looks sooner, not later.
newsitem.headline: Australian election looks sooner, not later.

text.p: Evidence is mounting that Australian Prime Minister John Howard will call an election in late 1998, well before the government's three-year term expires in the first half of 1999.

The government's own backbenchers have begun whispering about the possibility of an election as early as June, but a November-December poll appears more likely judging from comments made by Howard and his senior ministers.

The most recent indication came from Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer on Sunday, when he said in answer to a journalist's question that the government was still "a year-and-a-half out from the next election".
But Treasurer Peter Costello has given more conclusive evidence, saying late last month that 1998 was the natural time for the next election.
"There could well be another federal election next year," he told a business lunch last month.
"I think that (1998) would be the natural timing."
The rules about Australian election timing are complicated but for all practical purposes, an election cannot be held later than May 1999.
Elections are sometimes held after only two-and-a-half years but the two previous terms, in which Labor was in government, lasted almost as long as possible -- three years.
Howard himself said in April he believed the next election would be held in 15 to 18 months, but has since said it was two years away.
The government has threatened on several occasions to dissolve parliament and call an early election if the Senate, the upper house of parliament, blocked major legislation.

"If the Senate is going to give us a hard time on sensible measures we are putting up then we are entitled to stockpile them as double-dissolution triggers," Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith said in May.

Under the Australian constitution, both houses of parliament can be dissolved and an election called if the Senate twice rejects a piece of government legislation as long as there is a three-month gap between the two rejections.
The government does not hold a majority in the Senate and needs two additional votes to ensure the passage of legislation.
Training Minister David Kemp last week repeated an earlier implied threat that the government's work-for-the-dole scheme was a possible double dissolution trigger.

"(If they do reject the scheme), we'll put that legislation back again into the Senate and if they continue to reject it, then obviously it does become a potential trigger for a double dissolution election," Kemp said.
"I must say that we'd be happy to fight an election around that, as well as other issues."
Some government backbenchers believe the government will take this path, stockpiling several pieces of legislation and then forcing them through with a joint sitting of both houses.
The stockpile could include native title legislation, plans to exclude small business from unfair dismissal laws and a tightening of the immigration programme.
But others think this is less likely, saying the government will hold on until the opposition appears to be struggling.
"I think you'd find if there was a fortnight when Labor has had some real problems or when we are really on top, it will probably be called then," one backbencher told Reuters.
"I think, if the opportunity is there, it will be late 1998."
The government's standing in opinion polls fell heavily earlier this year but has recently recovered a little. But it has always been in a winning position.
